topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Low-level interfaces often provide raw buffers and callable addresses. Correct code must distinguish navigating existing objects, decoding bytes, and invoking different pointer categories. This chapter decodes a little-endian field without inventing an unaligned uint32_t object in a byte buffer, then compares an ordinary function pointer with pointers to data members and member functions.

blocks.text: A packet decoder crashes only when its input starts at an odd address. Another callback works until the object that supplied its state is destroyed. Both defects can be hidden behind syntactically valid pointer operations. The missing information is not the address alone: it is the bounds, type, alignment, lifetime, and ownership contract associated with that address.

blocks.text: HarborWorks will keep raw-pointer boundaries narrow. Inside the application, spans and ordinary typed interfaces carry enough structure to reason about access. At the boundary, explicit decoding and typed callback registration make assumptions visible. The objective is not to avoid every pointer, but to stop asking a pointer value to prove facts it does not contain.

topics.title: 7.1.1 Performing Pointer Arithmetic
topics.summary: Pointer arithmetic is defined in relation to an array object and its permitted one-past boundary. Adding an element count is not arbitrary address arithmetic across every mapped page. A span packages a pointer and count for a borrowed contiguous sequence and makes bounds available to an interface, though operator[] still relies on the caller’s valid index in the C++20 baseline.

topics.title: 7.1.2 Interpreting Raw Buffers
topics.summary: A buffer of bytes does not automatically contain a live object of whichever type a cast names. Reinterpreting its address as a typed pointer can violate alignment, lifetime, aliasing, or representation requirements. Decode protocol fields explicitly or use an appropriate representation-copy operation only when its type and lifetime conditions are established.

blocks.text: Explicit decoding also handles byte order and malformed input. A four-byte unsigned field can be reconstructed by converting bytes to a suitable unsigned type and shifting them into defined positions. Check length before accessing bytes, and define what trailing data means at the framing layer. A successful pointer cast is not validation.

blocks.text: A raw buffer is a sequence of storage units. It becomes meaningful only through an encoding contract. The worked decoder interprets four bytes as a little-endian unsigned field by converting each byte to an unsigned value and combining it at the specified shift position. It never invents a uint32_t object at the buffer’s starting address, so it does not need the buffer to satisfy that type’s alignment for a typed load.

blocks.text: The worked function accepts a span containing at least four bytes and decodes its first field. It is not a complete frame parser and does not reject every trailing byte. That is a deliberate layering decision: a field decoder and a message decoder have different contracts. When combining fields, the message layer must track how much input was consumed and decide whether extra data belongs to another field, another frame, or an error.

topics.title: 7.2.1 Working with Function Pointers
topics.summary: A function pointer identifies a compatible free or static function. Its type includes the function’s parameter and return types and relevant qualifiers. Calling through an incompatible signature is not a valid shortcut for generic dispatch. A null function pointer must be checked before invocation when absence is permitted.

blocks.text: Function pointers are useful for small dispatch tables or C interfaces, but they do not own captured state. A capturing lambda cannot generally convert to an ordinary function pointer because its closure carries an object. Use a suitable callable abstraction when stateful behavior is required, and document callback lifetime and exception boundaries.

blocks.text: A function pointer’s type states how the function can be called. Parameters, return type, and relevant qualifiers must agree with the actual function. Casting incompatible functions into one apparent signature does not make their calling conventions or argument interpretations compatible. A dispatch table should store functions sharing a deliberate interface rather than erase mismatches through casts.

blocks.text: A noncapturing lambda can often be used where a compatible ordinary function pointer is required. A capturing lambda carries state in a closure object and generally cannot be represented by a function address alone. This is a useful reminder that behavior and state can have separate lifetimes. std::function, templates, or an explicit function-plus-context design may be more appropriate when the callback needs captured data.

blocks.text: C-style APIs frequently pair a callback with an opaque context pointer. The pointer does not own the context. The application must ensure that the object survives every possible callback invocation, including callbacks racing with shutdown or deregistration. A safe registration object can make the subscription lifetime explicit, but its destructor must coordinate with in-flight callbacks according to the API’s rules rather than simply delete the context and hope no callback remains.

blocks.text: Exception boundaries deserve similar care. A callback invoked through a C interface or native event mechanism may not permit a C++ exception to escape. Catch failures at the adapter boundary and translate them into the interface’s supported error channel. Do not add a noexcept declaration merely to suppress concern: an escaping exception from a nonthrowing function leads to termination rather than an ordinary error result.

topics.title: 7.2.2 Working with Pointers to Members
topics.summary: A pointer to a data member describes a member relative to an object of a class, not an ordinary absolute address. A pointer to a member function similarly needs an object on which to invoke it. The .* and ->* operators apply these pointers, and std::invoke provides a uniform invocation interface for several callable forms.
